THE _I CHING_ AND _THE MAN IN THE HIGH CASTLE_ 

287 

## **Paul Mountfort** 

## **The** _**I Ching**_ **and Philip K. Dick’s** _**The Man in the High Castle**_ 

“I’ve used it to develop the direction of a novel.” —Philip K. Dick on the _I Ching_ (“Schizophrenia” 179) 

The Hugo Award-winning classic _The Man in the High Castle_ (1962) is widely regarded as Philip K. Dick’s breakthrough novel, and it remains among his most critically acclaimed. Its central premise has also proved to have longevity in popular culture: the pilot for the 2015 television adaptation was Amazon’s most watched program ever (“Amazon”). The novel’s central plot device is the main characters’ periodic use of the Chinese oracle or divination text known as the _I Ching_ or _Book of Changes_ . Dick appears to have consulted the oracle more or less obsessively to aid him in developing the direction of _High Castle_ , setting up a powerful metafictional dynamic between the author and his protagonists. Despite widespread acknowledgement of this compositonal technique and frequent mention of the role of the _I Ching_ in the construction of _High Castle_ , however, there has been little detailed analysis of it as a structuring or patterning device in the novel. While critics have praised _High Castle_ as a landmark example of the _uchronie_ or alternate-history genre, they have failed to perceive how deeply the text’s hidden symmetries were inspired by Dick’s use of the _I Ching_ . The cornerstone study in this area, Paul Williams’s essay “The Author and the Oracle” (1990), while valuable as the only systematic consideration of the oracular consultations that punctuate the story, was published over two decades ago, is hard to locate, and in my view seriously underestimates the _I Ching’s_ significant contributions to the novel, describing these as “not extensive” (5).
